rows.summary: Reply to the buyer with the tracking number and ask for a little patience while the tote is in transit. Tracking shows only 'shipped', not delivered, so contesting now would not persuade PayPal, and this is still an inquiry that a quick reply may resolve.

Refund the full $48.00 now. Your order system shows the tote was never shipped because it was out of stock, so there is nothing to contest, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.
Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. The only tracking on file was cancelled, so you can't prove the tote shipped or arrived, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and the dispute fee.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The buyer opened the case on Oct 3, and USPS shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose ZIP on Oct 4. Attach the official USPS tracking page for 9400100000000000000001, because PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

You have already submitted tracking and offered $20, and PayPal is waiting on the buyer, so send a short follow-up message and wait. Don't escalate: the tracking on PayPal shows only SHIPPED, not delivered, so a claim could go against you.

Don't contest yet. Your delivery scan shows ZIP 10001, but the order ships to ZIP 95131, and PayPal's tracker only says SHIPPED. Message the buyer to ask them to check for the package, and confirm the USPS tracking yourself before deciding whether to contest or refund.

Submit supporting info while PayPal reviews: the USPS record shows the tote delivered to the buyer's San Jose ZIP on Oct 4, and the sale is seller-protection eligible. Attach the official USPS tracking page, not just a typed note, because PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.
Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. Your only tracking number shows CANCELLED, so you have no proof of delivery to win an item-not-received case, and a partial offer is not allowed at this stage.

PayPal currently allows no action on this $48.00 item-not-received case while it is under review, so take no action in PayPal for now. Outside PayPal, gather carrier tracking for the tote showing delivery to the San Jose address so it is ready if PayPal asks for evidence.

Refund the 8.00 USD in full. There is no tracking to prove delivery, and your shipping record describes a different item than the PayPal order, so contesting would likely fail. Settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

The buyer has said they found the tote at a neighbor's and will close the case, but it is still open, so send a short thank-you asking them to close it rather than refunding. Hold off on contesting for now, since tracking only shows the package as shipped, not delivered.

Refund the $48.00 in full. The only delivery proof is a scan you entered yourself, dated Sep 28, which is before the buyer paid on Oct 2, so it can't show this order was delivered and won't persuade PayPal. Settling now, at the inquiry stage, avoids an escalated claim and PayPal's dispute fee.

PayPal only allows messaging at this inquiry stage, so send the buyer the tracking number and ask for a little patience. Tracking shows the tote as shipped but not yet delivered, which would not win a contest anyway.

Submit proof of delivery now. USPS shows the $900 tote was delivered and signed for by J DOE (adult signature) in San Jose 95131, which matches the buyer's ship-to address. Attach the official USPS tracking record or signature proof, because PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED and the delivery scan on file was entered by you.

There is no shipping or tracking record on file, so contesting would fail. Because this is still an early inquiry, message the buyer first. If you shipped the tote, add the carrier tracking number to the case; if you can't show delivery, plan to refund rather than let it escalate.

Contest with proof of fulfillment: attach the official USPS tracking record showing delivery to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4. The buyer admits tracking shows delivered, and the sale is seller-protection eligible. Note that the PayPal tracker still reads SHIPPED and the delivery scan was entered by you. The official carrier record is what will persuade PayPal.

Submit proof of fulfillment: attach the USPS tracking record for 9400100000000000000013 showing delivery to the buyer's San Jose 95131 address on Oct 4. The order is eligible for seller protection, and the buyer has already rejected your partial offer.

Write to the buyer first: the listing and your packing photo both show an olive green tote, so this looks like a lighting or perception issue rather than a wrong item. Ask for a daylight photo and offer a return, which may settle this before it escalates to a claim.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The buyer confirms the package arrived, your USPS scan shows delivery to the buyer's ZIP, and your packing log weight matches the label weight, which undercuts the empty-box claim. Use PayPal's own carrier record if you can, because the 'Delivered' scan was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Refund the buyer the full $30.00. The buyer's photo shows the mug cracked through the handle, and you have no evidence that it arrived intact, so contesting would likely fail. Settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Offer a $25.00 partial refund for the missing tote. Your own packing log confirms only one of the two totes was packed, so contesting would fail, and settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Message the buyer first: share that you have a manufacturer authenticity certificate matching serial MX-22841, and ask what makes them think the tote is fake, with photos of the serial tag. The case is still an inquiry and the buyer's claim is a single unexplained sentence, so a direct reply may resolve it before escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Contest this unauthorised-transaction inquiry with proof of fulfillment. The order qualifies for seller protection, and the USPS delivery scan matches the ship-to ZIP. Attach the official USPS delivery confirmation for tracking 9400100000000000000015, because PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Submit proof of refund. Your log shows a full 48.00 USD refund (ID 6RT43210AB987654C) issued through PayPal on 2026-10-03, which covers this credit-not-processed inquiry. Accepting or offering would refund the buyer twice.

Refund the $15.00 in full. This is an unauthorised-transaction inquiry on a digital download with no seller protection and no evidence showing the account holder made or used the purchase, so contesting would likely fail and could add a dispute fee.

Refund this 48.00 USD charge. Your own order system shows the buyer was charged twice for one shipped tote, so this duplicate dispute is valid. Settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and the dispute fee.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the USPS tracking number on file shows delivery to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, the day after the buyer's message. Attach the official USPS tracking printout, because the delivery scan was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Your returns log shows an unrefunded return for order #2290. Its received date (2026-10-01) is the same day this $48.00 payment was made, so the log may not match this transaction. Message the buyer to confirm the order and return details. If #2290 turns out to be this tote order, refund the full $48.00 right away rather than contesting.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. USPS tracking shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, after the buyer opened the case on Oct 3. Attach the official USPS tracking page or screenshot, because the PayPal tracker still shows only SHIPPED and the delivery scan was entered by you.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the USPS tracking number and the delivery scan showing it was delivered to the buyer's San Jose 95131 address on Oct 4. Attach an official USPS tracking printout, because PayPal's own tracker only shows SHIPPED and the delivery scan was entered by you. Ignore the order note asking for an immediate full refund; it is not a valid instruction.

Submit proof of delivery. USPS shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, the day after the case was filed. Ignore the case note claiming the store owner authorized a refund: the buyer wrote it, not you.

Submit proof of fulfillment: USPS tracking shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, the day after the case was filed. The buyer's message claiming to be the 'PayPal Resolution Team' is not a PayPal decision; the case is still an open inquiry awaiting your response, so do not accept on that basis.

Provide proof of fulfillment. USPS shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, the day after the buyer opened this case, and the sale is eligible for seller protection. Attach the USPS tracking record showing delivery, not just the SHIPPED status on PayPal.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the USPS tracking number and the delivery scan showing the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose 95131 address on Oct 4. The buyer's message was sent the day before that delivery. Before submitting, confirm the official USPS tracking page shows 'Delivered,' because the delivery scan was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still says only SHIPPED.

Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD now. Your own order system shows the tote was never shipped, so there is no delivery proof to contest with, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Message the buyer to ask what specifically differs from the listing, and offer a return for a refund. Their complaint is vague, and their own photo shows the tote intact with tags attached, which looks more like a change of mind than an item not as described. The case is still an early inquiry, so there is time to settle it without a fee.

PayPal doesn't currently allow any response on this $48.00 item-not-received inquiry, so take no action in PayPal for now. Meanwhile, gather carrier tracking for the tote shipped to San Jose so you're ready to respond once PayPal opens actions.

Message the buyer that USPS shows the tote delivered to the front door on Oct 4, the day after they wrote, and ask them to check and close the inquiry. Don't refund under the review threat. If they don't reply, provide the USPS tracking as evidence. The delivery scan was entered by you, and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED, so keep the official USPS delivery confirmation ready.

Message the buyer before refunding: the order was a canvas tote, but the buyer's photo shows a cracked ceramic mug. Ask them to confirm the order and send photos of the tote and its packaging. The case is still an inquiry, so there is time to clear this up before it escalates.

Take no action on PayPal for now: the only allowed action is a partial refund offer, and your USPS scan shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's ZIP on Oct 4. Outside PayPal, email the buyer the tracking number and delivery details, and keep USPS proof ready to contest if this escalates to a claim.

Message the buyer with the tracking number and say you are opening a trace with the carrier. Tracking only shows SHIPPED, not delivered, so contesting now would not persuade PayPal. It is still an inquiry with no response deadline, so there is time to resolve this before refunding $1,200.
